verses.text: Joash was seven years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Zibiah, of Beersheba.
Joash did that which was right in Yahweh’s eyes all the days of Jehoiada the priest.
Jehoiada took for him two wives, and he became the father of sons and daughters.
After this, Joash intended to restore Yahweh’s house.

He gathered together the priests and the Levites, and said to them, “Go out to the cities of Judah, and gather money to repair the house of your God from all Israel from year to year. See that you expedite this matter.” However the Levites didn’t do it right away.

The king called for Jehoiada the chief, and said to him, “Why haven’t you required of the Levites to bring in the tax of Moses the servant of Yahweh, and of the assembly of Israel, out of Judah and out of Jerusalem, for the Tent of the Testimony?”
For the sons of Athaliah, that wicked woman, had broken up God’s house; and they also gave all the dedicated things of Yahweh’s house to the Baals.
So the king commanded, and they made a chest, and set it outside at the gate of Yahweh’s house.
They made a proclamation through Judah and Jerusalem, to bring in for Yahweh the tax that Moses the servant of God laid on Israel in the wilderness.
All the princes and all the people rejoiced, and brought in, and cast into the chest, until they had filled it.

Whenever the chest was brought to the king’s officers by the hand of the Levites, and when they saw that there was much money, the king’s scribe and the chief priest’s officer came and emptied the chest, and took it, and carried it to its place again. Thus they did day by day, and gathered money in abundance.

The king and Jehoiada gave it to those who did the work of the service of Yahweh’s house. They hired masons and carpenters to restore Yahweh’s house, and also those who worked iron and brass to repair Yahweh’s house.
So the workmen worked, and the work of repairing went forward in their hands. They set up God’s house as it was designed, and strengthened it.

When they had finished, they brought the rest of the money before the king and Jehoiada, from which were made vessels for Yahweh’s house, even vessels with which to minister and to offer, including spoons and vessels of gold and silver. They offered burnt offerings in Yahweh’s house continually all the days of Jehoiada.
But Jehoiada grew old and was full of days, and he died. He was one hundred thirty years old when he died.
They buried him in David’s city among the kings, because he had done good in Israel, and toward God and his house.
Now after the death of Jehoiada, the princes of Judah came, and bowed down to the king. Then the king listened to them.
They abandoned the house of Yahweh, the God of their fathers, and served the Asherah poles and the idols, so wrath came on Judah and Jerusalem for this their guiltiness.
Yet he sent prophets to them, to bring them again to Yahweh, and they testified against them; but they would not listen.

The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “Thus says God, ‘Why do you disobey Yahweh’s commandments, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’”
They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of Yahweh’s house.
Thus Joash the king didn’t remember the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him, but killed his son. When he died, he said, “May Yahweh look at it, and repay it.”

At the end of the year, the army of the Syrians came up against him: and they came to Judah and Jerusalem, and destroyed all the princes of the people from among the people, and sent all their plunder to the king of Damascus.

For the army of the Syrians came with a small company of men; and Yahweh delivered a very great army into their hand, because they had forsaken Yahweh, the God of their fathers. So they executed judgment on Joash.

When they had departed from him (for they left him very sick), his own servants conspired against him for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest, and killed him on his bed, and he died. They buried him in David’s city, but they didn’t bury him in the tombs of the kings.
These are those who conspired against him: Zabad the son of Shimeath the Ammonitess and Jehozabad the son of Shimrith the Moabitess.

Now concerning his sons, the greatness of the burdens laid on him, and the rebuilding of God’s house, behold, they are written in the commentary of the book of the kings. Amaziah his son reigned in his place.

footnotes.content: A child-king, only seven—small hands for a heavy crown. Yet God placed him in Judah's seat. How often the Lord works through the young, not despite their youth, but because they have not yet learned to trust their own strength.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As long as Jehoiada stood near, Joash did right. What a gift—a wise elder to steady a young heart. I've learned that God often hides His grace in the counsel of faithful people around us. Follow them, and you follow Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoiada found Joash wives, and a house was built. The priest cared for the king's whole life—not just his worship, but his future, his family. This is the work of true shepherding, done quietly, without fanfare.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After settling, Joash's heart turned to restoration. There's a pattern here: receive faithfully, then give back to the Lord's house. The impulse to restore what's broken often rises in a heart that has known care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king commanded swift action, yet the Levites dragged their feet. Even good intentions face delays—people are slow to move, even toward God's work. Sometimes a push is needed, and that's not a flaw in leadership; it's the way of human hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joash had to ask why. The tax of Moses—ancient as Sinai itself—had fallen away. When we stop asking 'why haven't we?', we drift further from God. This young king learned that leadership sometimes means asking hard questions of those we trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Athaliah the wicked had gutted the Temple—tearing out vessels, breaking the sacred space itself. Now Joash sees the wreckage his predecessor left. He inherits not a throne, but a call to repair what was torn by pride and idolatry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A wooden chest, placed outside the Temple gate. So simple—a box, nothing ornate. Yet it became the vessel through which God's people gave, and through which His house was restored. The Lord often chooses humble means to do holy work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They proclaimed through all the cities the tax that Moses laid down in the wilderness—a law older than the land itself. Calling people back to ancient faithfulness, not to something new. The deepest reforms reach backward to the oldest truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Princes and people rejoiced and gave. When a leader's heart bends toward God, the people follow—not from duty, but from joy. They filled the chest because they saw their king loved the Lord's house more than his own wealth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Day by day they emptied the chest, counting, organizing, faithfully stewarding what the people gave. Such work is invisible, unglamorous—yet without it, no temple rises. God's kingdom moves on the backs of those who serve without seeking the spotlight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Masons, carpenters, workers in iron and brass—all laboring together. Each craft needed, each hand essential. The Temple's restoration teaches that God uses all kinds of skill and strength, united toward one sacred purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The work moved forward in their hands, and the house was set as it was designed and strengthened. I hear the satisfaction here—brokenness restored, the design honored, the foundation made firm. This is what happens when a people's hands and hearts align toward God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Finishing the repairs, they made vessels of gold and silver for the Temple's service. The renovation complete, worship could flourish—offerings burning continually before the Lord. Jehoiada saw the house of God restored in his lifetime, and so did his king.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One hundred thirty years old when Jehoiada died—a full life, long in faithfulness. He lived to see the young king grow, the Temple healed, judgment averted. What a gift to hold the line long enough to see God's restoration begin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Buried among the kings—not because he was royal by birth, but because he had done good toward God and His house. The highest honor goes not to the crowned, but to those who served faithfully. His grave became a monument to a life spent for the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoiada gone, the princes circled like wolves. They bowed to the young king—not from respect, but to turn him. Without a guardian's voice, even a faithful heart can be swayed by flatterers who smell opportunity. This is how good reigns crumble.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They abandoned the Lord and served wooden poles. So quick the turning—from restoration to apostasy, from the God who made them to carved wood. And God's wrath came, not in rage, but in the natural consequence of forsaking Him. He withdraws, and all falls.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord sent prophets—men to stand and call them back. Even in judgment, He did not leave them voiceless. He always sends messengers before He sends swords. Yet they would not listen. How many times does He speak before we finally hear?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Spirit came upon Zechariah, Jehoiada's own son, and he stood before the people with a hard word: 'Why do you disobey? Because you've forsaken God, He has forsaken you.' It was the faithful son of the faithful elder, carrying the father's work. Yet faithfulness in a corrupt court is often a lonely calling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They stoned him in the Temple court—killed the prophet at the king's command, at Yahweh's own house. The place that had been restored with such joy became a tomb for the faithful. Injustice often strikes where holiness is most conspicuous.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joash forgot all that Jehoiada had done for him—raised him, stabilized his reign, guided his heart—and repaid it with the death of Jehoiada's son. Ingratitude is the hardest sin; it cuts the bond of grace. With his last breath, the dying king appealed to the Lord for justice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Syrian army came at year's end—a small force, yet it swept through, destroyed the princes, plundered the people. The God who had once given victory now withdrew His hand. A nation that forgets Him finds itself defenseless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They were outnumbered, yet God gave the enemy victory—such a reversal. The Lord delivered judgment into the Syrians' hands because Judah had forsaken Him. This is the weight of apostasy: heaven itself turns against us. Yet even judgment is His voice, calling us back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His own servants—men he should have trusted—conspired and killed him on his sickbed, avenging Zechariah's blood. The man who forgot kindness found himself without it. He was buried in the city of David, but denied the tombs of kings. His grave was a rebuke.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The conspirators are named—Zabad and Jehozabad, sons of foreign mothers. History marks them, not as heroes, but as men who took up bloodshed to settle old wrongs. Human memory holds grudges longer than God does, and vengeance spirals on and on.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The story is written in the annals—all of it, the high calling and the terrible fall. Readers today hear an echo: how quickly a heart can shift from serving the Lord to abandoning Him, from receiving grace to forgetting it. We see Joash and recognize ourselves—and that recognition is itself a mercy, calling us to hold fast.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
